description:
Chasqui Health

In the Inca Empire, chasquis were runners who carried vital messages across vast distances. I’m bringing that idea to space: a tool that carries the health of a crew back to Earth.

I’m building Astronaut Health, a space health monitor with an interactive 3D body, Normal/Watch/Critical alerts, trends and gamified check-ins. Solo developer from Lima, Peru, always happy to exchange ideas and feedback with other teams.
summary:
Quipu  Health helps crew members assess and act on their own health when help
from Earth is delayed. Crew log vitals, symptoms and wellbeing; the app compares them
with reference thresholds and each astronaut's pre-flight baseline, colors an
interactive 3D body map by status (normal, watch, critical), explains why, and
suggests an action. For critical states it prepares a report for the flight surgeon
and shows the communication delay of the selected environment (ISS, Moon or Mars).
It adds daily measurement reminders, a transparent health score, NASA HRP-based risk
tracking and live space weather from NASA DONKI. Physiological data is simulated.
This is an educational prototype, not a medical device.
details:
THE PROBLEM

On long missions to the Moon and Mars, astronauts are exposed to radiation,

isolation, altered gravity and closed environments, and Earth is far away. NASA's

Human Research Program (HRP) groups these into five hazards. With delayed

communication, crews carry much of the responsibility for noticing changes in

themselves and deciding what to do.

OUR SOLUTION

Quipu Health is a visual tool that gathers health indicators, interprets them

and guides the next step.

- Vitals and wellbeing: blood pressure, heart rate, glucose, body temperature, sleep,

mood, reaction time, meals completed and social contact, plus a daily check-in

and a symptom checker (rash, vision changes, dizziness).

- Interactive 3D body map: each zone is colored normal, watch or critical, with the

reason ("Under watch due to: sleep hours"), the indicators behind it and a

recommended action. The overall status follows the worst indicator.

- Baselines and thresholds: readings are compared with reference thresholds and

with an optional pre-flight baseline for each astronaut.

- Routine: daily reminders for pending measurements and light gamification to

encourage consistent self-monitoring.

- Escalation: in a critical state the app prepares a report for the flight surgeon

and shows the one-way communication delay for the chosen environment.

- Explanations: a rule-based flight surgeon summarizes the last 7 days, and a

health score shows exactly which rules lowered it.

- Mission risks: the five HRP hazards, study tracking inspired by NASA HRP studies

(Immune Biomarkers, SANS/B-Complex, CIPHER, ARCHeR) and a pre-EVA checklist.

NASA DATA AND SOURCES

- Live data: space weather events from the NASA DONKI API, used as risk context.

- NASA HRP: the five hazards and the risk pages shaped the indicators, the risk

panel and the explanations. The study-tracking tab follows the HRP studies listed

in the references.

- Reference thresholds come from AHA (blood pressure), ADA (glucose) and WHO

(hypertension). [Add sources for CO2, calories and radiation values.]

- Canadian Space Agency pages on the effects of spaceflight back some explanations.

- Physiological readings are simulated: real astronaut vitals are not openly

available, and NASA Standard Measures data is access-controlled.

IMPACT

Deeper missions mean longer delays and less support from Earth. A tool that helps a

crew interpret its own data, know when to escalate and keep a monitoring routine

supports the autonomy those missions need. The approach also applies on Earth in

isolated settings with limited access to specialists. The Canadian Space Agency notes

that space health research has benefited conditions such as osteoporosis,

cardiovascular disorders and type 2 diabetes.

CREATIVITY

- The body itself is the dashboard: color-coded zones on a 3D model, with causes

and actions attached to each zone, instead of a table of numbers.

- Escalation that accounts for communication delay by environment.

- Transparent rules: the status, the score and the recommendations show their

reasoning.

- Routine support (reminders, streaks, quick reaction test) to keep crews measuring.

VALIDITY AND LIMITATIONS

- Decisions come from explicit rules and cited thresholds, so every result can be

explained and checked. The "flight surgeon" is rule-based, not an AI model.

- Not a medical device: it records, suggests and escalates; it does not diagnose.

Thresholds are general adult references and would need validation by flight

surgeons.

- All physiological data is simulated, and values like radiation dose and delay

are simulated mission values.

- It covers only what a crew member can measure alone. Blood counts, bone density,

imaging and intracranial pressure need laboratory or dedicated equipment.

- [Include only if implemented: entries are checked for plausibility. Impossible

values are rejected, extreme but possible ones ask for confirmation and trigger a

critical alert instead of being blocked.]

BUILT WITH

Ruby on Rails 8.1, Hotwire (Turbo, Stimulus), Three.js, Chart.js, Tailwind CSS,

Propshaft. Hosted on Render. 3D model: "Ecorche - Anatomy study" by Beatriz Gomez

Santamaria (CC BY 4.0), modified to color zones by status.
